messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert Hale was 76, a European American man living alone after a long divorce, and he had spent most of his working life managing a hotel in a busy Midwestern city. The event that now governed his days had taken place years earlier in the hotel’s basement maintenance corridor, when a storage area for cleaning supplies was mishandled and he was suddenly engulfed by a sharp chemical odor that stung his eyes, burned his throat, and made him feel as if his body had turned against him. He remembered stumbling toward the stairwell, unable to make sense of what he was breathing, with coworkers shouting somewhere above him and the corridor seeming to shrink around him. What stayed with Robert was not a tidy story but broken pieces: the sight of a mop bucket overturned on the concrete floor, the metallic taste in his mouth, the terrible smell that returned later in flashes, and, at other times, only the full wave of terror without any image at all. When he tried to think about it, the memory arrived in fragments that did not fit together, and sometimes the smell was so vivid he would grimace and cover his nose as if it were happening again.

In the months after the exposure, Robert began to treat his own body as unreliable, then as an enemy. He was certain that if his chest tightened or his stomach turned, it meant danger was already present, and he could not trust himself to tell the difference between memory and reality. That conviction made him constantly scan his body and his thoughts, waiting for the first sign that he was “going crazy” or that the chemical had done lasting damage. The more he noticed those sensations, the more convinced he became that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He began feeling on guard even inside his own home, and certain places in the house—a chair by the window, the laundry room, the narrow hall near the basement door—felt like the only safe zones in a world that had become too large and too uncertain. Unexpected or loud sounds, especially a radiator clank or a car backfiring outside his apartment building, made him jump and stay tense for minutes afterward. His fear was not abstract; it was tied to the belief that his own body might betray him again without warning, and that the danger could appear anywhere.

Those sensations, and the half-formed memories behind them, also changed the way Robert handled his days. If a smell or a bodily flutter brought back that wash of terror, he would turn on the television or blast old music just to fill the room and keep his mind from settling on what he might feel next. He watched his thoughts closely, checking and rechecking them for signs that he was losing control, and if a fragment of the incident surfaced—a smell, a flash of the basement corridor, the scrape of work shoes on concrete—he would distract himself immediately rather than let it develop. At the hotel, where he still works part-time on familiar administrative tasks, he avoids the basement and the maintenance routes whenever he can, asking younger staff to handle anything that would take him near the old storage areas. He tells himself this is common sense, yet the relief is short-lived. The more he listens for every internal sensation and every unexpected sound, the more easily his body seems to react, and the more he becomes convinced that something is still wrong with him. In his view, the loud music and constant checking are attempts to stay in control, but they have also reinforced the sense that he is fragile and must monitor himself to keep disaster at bay.

By the time he came for help, Robert had become smaller in his own life. He had stopped meeting friends after work because restaurants and crowded lobbies felt too exposed, and he had begun arranging his errands around the few places that still felt tolerable. The memory still intruded in pieces, the smell still arrived when he least expected it, and every one of those moments tightened his sense that danger was near and his body could not be trusted. What finally brought him in was his worry that the circle had become unlivable: he was spending more time guarding against signs of catastrophe than actually living, and he feared that if he did not get help he would remain trapped in a world that felt unsafe everywhere except in a handful of rooms. He wanted, more than anything, to trust his body again and to stop feeling as though disaster was always about to begin.
